findings.where: First screen, the blue field behind everything (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: The direction is meant to be one calm field of house blue, but the field is covered in diagonal hatch stripes. The stripes make the ground busy behind the large white line and the lead paragraph. They read as a warning pattern or a technical drawing's shading, not as a quiet colour. The page also contradicts itself. The Texture tile says 'No texture: one flat field, no grain and no gradient', and the motion sketch shows the field flat, yet the real first screen is striped.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who judges the first screen first. He asked for the ground's busyness to be decided with care and for nothing to read as 'in-your-face techy'. Mark, who finds busy sites off-putting (brand sheet §6). A development-bank reader, for whom the stripes add noise to the message with no meaning behind it.

findings.where: First screen, the large ghosted 'PPP' letters behind the heading (desktop; on phone, cut off at the right edge behind the heading)
findings.fault: A second display element sits behind Mark's line and competes with it. The giant pale 'PPP' shows through the white heading's letters, so the one large serif line is no longer the only big thing on the screen. It reads as a watermark gimmick. On phone it is cropped into a meaningless fragment behind the words.
findings.who_objects: The founder: the research asks for scale contrast from one very large line, not from more elements, and the brief calls for refined, never novelty. A first-time reader, whose eye snags on the faint letterforms while reading the heading.

findings.where: Article specimen: the image caption and the subhead 'So, what are the key 'chapter topics'?', the three-item list, and the PDF row under it (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: The specimen fails at the very thing the brief asks it to show, a rhythm that holds when Angélique adds an image, caption, list and subhead. The subhead sits tight against the photo caption, so it reads as part of the image group rather than as the start of the next section. The list is set much tighter than the paragraphs around it, so its lines crowd together and look like a different text. The list's last line runs straight into the rule and the PDF link, with no breathing space.
findings.who_objects: The founder and the round-1 critics, who made the rhythm under real content a condition of this round. Angélique, who will add exactly these elements. A reader, who loses which heading belongs to which part of the article.

findings.where: First screen on phone, the action 'Write to me at Mark.Moseley@MMMinfra.com'
findings.fault: On a phone, the first screen is the logo, the nav, the portrait and the start of the heading. The one action falls well below the first screen, after the heading, the lead paragraph and the topic line. The brief's 'one message and one action on the first screen' holds on desktop but not on phone.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank officer opening the site from a LinkedIn link on a phone. They see Mark's face and his line but no way to write to him until they scroll past two blocks of text. Only the small 'Contact' nav item offers the action within reach.

findings.where: First screen, the topic line 'PPP Law · Infrastructure · Development banks · Governments · Risk allocation' between the lead paragraph and the action (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: A third, smaller tier of text sits between the message and the action. It is a list of keywords that repeats what the lead paragraph has just said ('development banks', 'governments', 'infrastructure'). It reads like a firm's list of services or a set of SEO tags, not like Mark's voice, and it adds clutter where the eye should go straight from the line to the address. On phone it wraps so that a lone middot starts the second line.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who asked for one message and one action and for a personal advisor, not a look any consultancy could own. A reader, who has to skim past the repeated terms on the way to the action.

findings.where: First screen as a whole (the homepage hero), desktop and phone
findings.fault: Nothing on the first screen shows evidence of Mark's work. There is no named body he has advised, no region of his work and no newest article or talk with its venue, only the claim in the lead paragraph. The hero tells a reader who Mark is and what he does, but not why to trust him.
findings.who_objects: Procurement-minded staff at multilateral development banks, who judge an advisor by checkable work and region (first-visit trust items 3, 4 and 6, 'Feel the CV'). They have no reason yet to write rather than keep looking.

findings.where: Below the fold, the Type pair row: 'In my view, Gelasio' on the left and 'Source Sans 3' on the right (desktop)
findings.fault: The two halves of the type pair do not line up. 'Source Sans 3' starts lower than the Gelasio specimen beside it, so it floats in its column and reads as if it belongs to the article section below rather than to the pair. The Palette and Texture row above lines up its tops, so this row looks careless next to it.
findings.who_objects: The founder, comparing the tiles: a loose specimen grid makes a style tile look less finished, in a round asked to be refined.
